Muscular Dystrophies
Definitions
A disease of muscle tissue is termed a myopathy.
Muscular dystrophies are heterogeneous conditions of genetic origin that typically result in
varying degrees and patterns of muscle weakness and degeneration of muscle tissue (Table
1).
Muscular dystrophies are rare; the prevalence is 19.8 to 25.1 cases per 100,000 individuals.1
The population, time of presentation, and severity may differ depending on the gene mutation
characteristics and the affected target protein.
Dystrophinopathies, including Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies, are the most
common types of muscular dystrophy.
The genetic mutation associated with both diseases occurs at the same location in the
dystrophin gene, and it includes the data to form a protein called dystrophin.
Other dystrophinopathies include the following:
Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD)
Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies (LGMDs)
Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD)

Definitions
Myopathies are commonly divided into inherited diseases and acquired conditions.
Inherited myopathies include conditions such as muscular dystrophies, mitochondrial
myopathies, ion channel disorders, glycogen storage disorders, and fatty acid oxidation
disorders. Acquired myopathies include inflammation (autoimmune) myopathies,
infectious myopathies, endocrine myopathies, and myopathies associated with a toxic
agent.
Dystrophin is a cytoskeletal protein located on the inner (cytoplasmic) side of the
myocyte membrane. Dystrophin is critical to cellular membrane stability and links the
actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. The presence of dystrophin prevents the
myocyte membrane from collapsing during a muscle contraction. If dystrophin is
missing, the cellular membrane becomes weakened and compromised, leading to an
unregulated calcium influx that eventually leads to muscle cell necrosis.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a rare disease, with an incidence of 1 in 3,500 live
male births2 and a prevalence of 1.7 to 4.2 per 100,000 individuals.1
DMD is the most common form of inherited muscle disease in childhood.
DMD is characterized by progressive deterioration of muscle mass and replacement by
fibroadipose tissue during childhood.
Pathogenesis
DMD is an X-linked recessive disease.
A genetic link can be identified in most cases (approximately 70%); the remainder of cases are
the result of de novo mutation.3
Mutations occur in the dystrophin gene, which is located on the Xp21 region of the X
chromosome and spans 2 million base pairs.
Mutations often (65% of patients) are caused by deletion of a segment of the gene that
interrupts the normal triplet sequence of the DNA, leading to a frameshift-type mutation and
formation of nonsense dystrophin that undergoes rapid degradation.4
In 15% of the patients, a single nucleotide mutation leads to a premature stop codon. This
mutation causes the cellular ribosome to stop transcribing the RNA, and proteins that were
made are degraded. Other gene abnormalities, including duplications and splice-site
mutations, may be responsible for other genetic-related errors.
Dystrophin mutation may result in the absence (or insufficient levels) of dystrophin protein in
muscle tissue, which leads to an inability to shield muscle from mechanical stress during
repeated contractions.
Cell injury and death leads to a prolonged inflammation process and ultimately, fibrosis and
fat deposition of the muscles.
Clinical Presentation
Typically, severe clinical manifestations of DMD are observed in males because of the X-linked
inheritance pattern.
The first symptoms usually appear between age 2 to 3 years.
In the first few years of life, muscle regeneration is excellent; however, as the child ages (4 to 6
years), muscle tissue degeneration outpaces the child’s ability to replace it, and clinically
evident signs and symptoms occur.
Signs and symptoms may include the following:

Delay in motor milestones, commonly delayed walking
Symmetric proximal lower-limb muscle weakness (hip extensors, abductors) with difficulty
running, ascending stairs, hopping on one leg, and rising from the floor (Gowers sign).
The Gowers sign is present if a child uses his or her hands to walk up to his legs and push off
the trunk into an upright standing position (Figure 1).
Abnormal gait: broad-based, Trendelenburg, or toe-walking
Clumsiness
Increased lumbar lordosis
Pseudohypertrophy of the calves (from muscle infiltration by connective tissue; Figure 2)
As the disease advances, signs and symptoms may include the following:
Flexion contractures of the hips and knees
Equinus contractures of the ankles
Scoliosis (often at thoracolumbar region, resistant to brace management)
Scoliosis develops in 95% of patients with DMD after transitioning to a wheelchair (usually
at approximately age 10 to 12 years). The scoliosis is characterized by long sweeping curves
and typically is relentlessly progressive.
Lumbar hyperlordosis may occur (mostly related to hip flexion contractures).
Proximal muscle weakness in the upper limbs
Shoulder weakness manifests as difficulty with shoulder elevation during feeding. Upper
limb involvement usually trails the lower limbs in weakness by 3 to 5 years.
Extra-orthopaedic manifestations include involvement of cardiac muscle.
Dystrophin protein also is found in cardiac muscle tissue; therefore, patients with DMD are
at risk for dilated cardiomyopathy.
The natural course of DMD is characterized by a progressive decline in muscle strength,
requiring the use of a wheelchair, typically by age 13 to 14 years.
The disease is inevitably fatal; cardiac and respiratory failure will lead to early mortality in
individuals in their twenties.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis often is delayed a couple years from the time a patient is first seen by a consulting
physician.
A high index of suspicion for DMD should be maintained in patients with the following:
Unexplained increase in serum transaminase level
A positive family history in the setting of abnormal muscle function
Boys with a delay in motor development, specifically if not walking by age 16 to 18 months
Serum creatine kinase levels serve as a screening test (may be as much as 10 to 200 times the
normal level).
DMD is confirmed via genetic testing, usually a cheek swab obtained to test for the dystrophin
gene.
Muscle biopsy may aid in diagnosis in the few patients in whom the diagnosis cannot be made
via genetic testing.
Prenatal diagnosis of DMD also is possible via amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling.

Management
No curative medical treatment option is available for DMD.
Multidisciplinary care is essential in the management of DMD.

Management
The care team should include an orthopaedic surgeon, neurologist, physiotherapist,
social worker, cardiologist, and pulmonologist. Consultations with the latter two are
particularly important before orthopaedic surgical treatment or at later stages as
patients experience cardiopulmonary decline. Treatment goals include preservation of
function, maintenance of bone health, prevention and reduction of contractures,
posture maintenance, and improvement of cardiac and pulmonary function.
Nonsurgical Management
Physical therapy and orthotic use
Physical therapy includes muscle stretching and range-of-motion exercises to prevent or
minimize contractures. Orthosis use usually is combined with the physical therapy. Orthoses
facilitate walking and assist during longer distances.
Corticosteroids (prednisone)
Corticosteroids alter the natural history of the disease by delaying the muscle degeneration
process and slowing disease progression.3 Steroids improve muscle strength, delay loss of
ambulation, preserve upper limb and respiratory functions, slow scoliosis progression, and
decrease the need for spinal fusion for scoliosis.5,6 Glucocorticoid therapy commonly is
initiated after age 4 to 5 years and continued for the patient’s entire life. Prolonged
glucocorticoid therapy is associated with severe adverse effects. Common adverse effects
include severe delays in growth, weight gain, osteonecrosis, cataracts, and osteopenia.
Synthetic corticosteroids equivalents
Deflazacort is a corticosteroid prodrug, with active metabolite that act through the
glucocorticoid receptor to exert anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects. It is
administered for patients aged 2 years or older. It is associated with less weight gain than
prednisone. In addition, deflazacort is associated with improved preservation of ambulation

Vamorolone is a dissociative steroid that aims to retain anti-inflammatory benefits with fewer

Nonsteroidal therapy
Duvyzat (Italfarmo SpA) is a histone deacetylase inhibitor that targets disease mechanisms to
reduce inflammation and muscle loss. It is approved for all genetic variants of DMD (in
patients aged 6 or older).
Gene therapy
Delandistrogene moxeparvovec-rokl is a gene therapy treatment for DMD. It delivers a
shortened version of the dystrophin gene to muscle cells, aiming to slow disease
progression. It initially was approved for all ambulatory patients aged 4 years or older who
have a confirmed DMD gene mutation.
Exon-skipping drugs recognize different exons in the pre-mRNA sequence, excluding exons
during mRNA processing, allowing mRNA-reading to become in-frame and allow for functional
protein formation.
Eteplirsen is the first disease-modifying drug for DMD. It recognizes and acts on exon 51.
Golodirsen and viltolarsen are directed at exon 53.
Casimersen targets exon 45.
Nonsense mutation therapy
Ataluren is meant for patients with DMD caused by a nonsense mutation. It targets a stop
codon in the mature mRNA of the dystrophin gene. It blocks the stop codon and allows
mRNA translation to be completed so a functional protein is produced.
Surgical Management
Surgical management of DMD is mainly performed for soft-tissue contractures and scoliosis.
Several anesthetic factors must be considered. Malignant hyperthermia is associated with
muscular dystrophies. The use of succinylcholine and inhalational agents is avoided
intraoperatively; patients may be pretreated with the use of dantrolene.
Contractures are managed via soft-tissue releases.
Specific procedures
Release of the iliotibial band to manage hip abduction contractures
Release of the sartorius, rectus femoris, and tensor fascia lata to manage hip flexion
contractures

Hamstring releases to manage knee flexion contracture
Achilles tendon lengthening to manage ankle equinus and toe walking
Posterior tibialis lengthening to manage flexible hindfoot varus
Soft-tissue releases in ambulatory patients are indicated to produce braceable feet and
preserve ambulation for as long as possible. In nonambulatory patients, treatment is
directed at maintaining a comfortable sitting position and joint range of motion and
decreasing the risk of fractures.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis is managed via posterior spine instrumented fusion if the patient is deemed fit for
surgical treatment. Posterior spine instrumented fusion maintains an upright posture and
decreases the work of breathing.
Indications are nonambulatory patients with scoliosis of more than 20° to 30° who have a
forced vital capacity more than 40% of normal.
A short window of opportunity exists for spinal fusion before the patient becomes too
debilitated for surgical treatment.
Bracing is mostly ineffective in the management of scoliosis in patients with DMD.
Becker Muscular Dystrophy
Overview
Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) is the second most common type of dystrophinopathy.
The prevalence of BMD is estimated to be 0.4 to 3.6 per 100,000 individuals.1
Pathogenesis
BMD is a recessive, X-linked disease.
The mutation is at the Xp21 locus on the X chromosome; this results in a milder phenotypic
expression than DMD.
The severity of the disease depends on the quantity of functional dystrophin protein in the
muscle cells.

Clinical Presentation
The onset of BMD occurs at a later age than the onset of DMD. Patients usually are
diagnosed at approximately age 7 years. Most patients remain ambulatory into early
adulthood (mean, 27 years). Patients with BMD survive into their forties.
Diagnosis
Laboratory analysis shows moderately elevated creatine kinase levels.
Genetic testing is the mainstay of disease confirmation.
Management
The goals of the orthopaedic management of BMD are similar to those for DMD; however,
management is initiated at a later patient age because of the relatively later and prolonged
clinical course of BMD.
In the past few years, promising developments in BMD research have been made, especially in
the fields of targeted therapy and personalized medicine. Despite encouraging clinical trial
data, no newly approved disease-modifying therapies currently are available for BMD.

Overview
EDMD is a rare inherited condition with a prevalence of 0.1 to 0.4 per 100,000 individuals.1

Pathogenesis
EDMD primarily affects the production of proteins associated with the nuclear membrane of
cells in skeletal and cardiac muscles.7

Pathogenesis
The most common mutation occurs at the STA gene located in the Xq28 region of the X
chromosome. The mutation affects the production of emerin protein, an inner nuclear
membrane protein that helps anchor the cell membrane to the cytoskeleton. Although
ubiquitous, emerin is more highly represented in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Other
forms of mutation (autosomal dominant and recessive) occur via the lamin-A/lamin-C
genes. Lamin-A and Lamin-C are intermediate filaments in the nuclear membrane and
nucleoplasm of most cells and contribute to the nuclear shape. They are essential for
DNA replication and mRNA transcription within the cell.
Clinical Presentation
EDMD presents in individuals in their teenage years.
Slowly progressive muscle wasting and weakness lead to early contractures.
Primarily affects the muscles of the arms, legs (humeroperoneal), and neck.
Scoliosis often is characterized by a slowly progressive curve.
Substantial risk of severe cardiac complications, including malignant ventricular arrhythmias,
and end-stage heart failure
Cardiac arrhythmias (heart block) are common, and sudden cardiac death is a frequent cause
of mortality.

Clinical Presentation
Cervical extension contractures (of longissimus capitis, longissimus cervicis, spinalis,
semispinalis, and suboccipitalis) limit cervical flexors (longus colli and longus capitis);

Diagnosis
In males, blood creatine kinase levels are elevated; in females, creatine kinase levels usually
are within normal limits.
Skin biopsy to determine the presence or absence of emerin has been proposed as a
diagnostic test.
Management
No specific treatment option exists for EDMD. Treatment strategies are tailored to the specific
symptoms in each patient. Physical therapy is recommended to prevent contractures. Surgical
management may be considered in select patients to manage limb joint contractures and, in
rare cases, cervical contractures.
Regular cardiac investigation and follow-up is warranted because arrythmias (and sudden
death) may occur in these patients. Early detection pacemakers or defibrillator implants may
be lifesaving.
Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophies
Overview
LGMD refers to a group of genetic muscle disorders characterized by reduced or absent
expression of specific muscle proteins (eg, sarcoglycans).
The estimated prevalence of LGMD is 0.9 to 2.3 in 100,000 individuals.1
Pathogenesis
The disease is commonly divided based on the pattern of inheritance into autosomal
dominant and autosomal recessive types.
Currently, eight subtypes of LGMD type 1 (autosomal dominant) and 26 subtypes of LGMD
type 2 (autosomal recessive) exist.

Type 2 (autosomal recessive) variants are more common (approximately 90%) than type 1


Pathogenesis
Type 2A is the most common LGMD. The mutation is located on chromosome 15 and
affects calpain-3 protein production. Type 2B involves a mutation on chromosome 2p13
and affects dysferlin, a transmembrane protein typically located in the sarcolemma. Type
2C through type 2F are known as the sarcoglycanopathies. Type 2I involves mutations in
fukutin-related protein.
Clinical Presentation
May be observed in males and females
Mostly affects shoulder or pelvic girdle muscles, with a phenotypic variation that depends on
the type and severity of deficiency of the protein
The onset and severity of the disease and the progression rate vary between different
subtypes of LGMD.
In general, the disease presents in individuals aged 0 to 19 years.
Muscle wasting
Pelvic girdle weakness usually involves the iliopsoas, gluteus maximus, and quadriceps
muscles.
Shoulder weakness usually involves the trapezius, rhomboids, latissimus dorsi, serratus
anterior, and the pectoralis major.
Progressive weakness of hip muscles (abductors and extensors) leads to increased lumbar
lordosis.
Patients with type 1A LGMD commonly present with a dysarthric pattern of speech.
Diagnosis
Creatine kinase levels may be normal or elevated.
Immunoassay analysis of muscle tissue searching for muscular dystrophy–associated proteins
Molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

Management
The mainstay of management is based on the specific symptoms. Physical therapy may help
prevent the onset and progression of contractures and promote mobility.
The value of corticosteroids is questionable, and no consensus exists on benefit of
management for the different subtypes of the disease.
Molecular-based treatment options are being developed to target genetic mutations; however,
they are in clinical trial stages.
Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy
Overview
FSHD is the third most common muscular dystrophy, with a prevalence of 3.2 to 4.6 per
100,000 individuals.1
Pathogenesis
Mutations related to FSHD primarily affect DNA packaging, leading to exposure of usually
silenced genes and their translation into abnormal proteins that damage the muscle.
Type 1 (70% to 90% of cases) is autosomal dominant and is associated with mutations on
chromosome 4q35.
The mutations cause a reduction in the number of copies of a repeated noncoding region
named D4Z4. This region affects silencing genes that are toxic to skeletal muscle (ie, double
homeobox 4 retrogene). An alteration in the number of D4Z4 regions changes double
homeobox 4 translation, and disease severity depends on the amount of double homeobox
4 transcribed.9
Type 2 is sporadic and related to de novo mutations
Mutations are associated with a packaging protein named SMCHD1, which leads to
transcription of muscle-toxic proteins.
Clinical Presentation
Males usually are more severely affected; however, FSHD also may be observed in females.
Symptoms typically begin between age 0 to 29 years and have a slower progression.
Symptoms include the following:

Facial weakness
Ankle and toe extensor weakness (footdrop)
Arm and shoulder girdle weakness, often with a winged scapula and limited arm abduction
This occurs later in the course of the disease. Affected muscles of the shoulder girdle
include the trapezius, rhomboids, and levator scapulae. Affected arm muscles include the
biceps, triceps, pectoral.
The Beevor sign: an upward movement of the umbilicus with neck flexion
Spinal hyperlordosis: observed in approximately one-third of patients
Extra-muscular manifestations include the following:
Atrial arrhythmias
Sensorineural hearing loss
Retinal telangiectasias
Restrictive respiratory disease
Seizures
Patients with FSHD usually have a normal life span.
Facial weakness usually is the earliest manifestation; other symptoms include difficulty
drinking through a straw or whistling, lack of wrinkles on the forehead and around the eyes,
incomplete eye closure (mostly observed during sleep), and a transverse smile.
Diagnosis
Creatine kinase levels typically are within the normal range.
Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
Management
Currently, no pharmacologic disease-modifying treatment options are available for FSHD.
Surgical management primarily targets stabilization of the shoulder girdle.
Scapulothoracic fusion may improve abduction and elevation of the upper extremities.

Pathogenesis
Mutations of the peripheral nerve may lead to motor and sensory deficits. The two main
resultant pathologic processes are demyelination, leading to decreased conduction
velocities, and axonal damage with Wallerian degeneration, reducing the transmission of
action potentials.
Clinical Presentation
The onset of symptoms typically is noted during the first and second decades of life but may
be observed later in patients with a milder form of the disease.
Males and females are equally affected; boys tend to have a more pronounced disease.
The typical clinical phenotype of CMT disease is characterized by progressive, often bilateral,
distal limb weakness with intrinsic muscle imbalance and symmetric distal sensory loss.
Neuropathic pain, particularly in the lower limbs and lumbar spine, is a common symptom of
CMT disease.
Patients often experience a decline in function from muscle imbalance, neuropathic pain, or
fatigue.

Clinical Presentation
Clinically, the feet usually are affected first. A relatively stronger peroneus longus
overpowers the tibialis anterior, and weak intrinsic muscles cause first ray plantar
flexion. The longitudinal arch is elevated with a contracted plantar fascia, and a cavus
foot posture is formed. This increases pressure on the metatarsal heads and leads to
painful calluses along the lateral border of the foot and beneath the metatarsal heads.
The weakened intrinsic muscles, which regularly flex the metatarsophalangeal joint and
extend the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of the foot, in combination with an
unopposed flexor digitorum longus and a flexor hallucis longus, create flexion
deformities of the interphalangeal joints to form a claw posture of the toes. The
relatively stronger posterior tibialis and peroneus longus with the weak peroneus brevis
contribute to the hindfoot varus, which is initially caused by plantar flexion of the first
ray, pushing the heel into varus (Figures 3 and 4).
Patients with CMT disease have a higher risk for acetabular dysplasia and hip
subluxation than the unaffected population. Dysplasia of the hip occurs in 5% to 10% of
all patients with CMT disease.11 This has been proposed to result from weakness in the
proximal musculature, including the hip abductor and extensor muscles. This may lead
to degenerative arthritis in adulthood.

atrophy of the small muscles of the hands, hyporeflexia or areflexia of the deep tendons,
scoliosis, and pes cavovarus. EMG/nerve conduction studies show very slow nerve
conduction velocities.

90% of patients have a positive family history.

the diagnosis.

Pediatric Traumatic Brain Injury
Overview
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) may cause serious disabilities and death.
TBI is defined as a disruption of brain activity or architecture caused by an external
biomechanical force directed onto the head.
An estimated 475,000 individuals aged 0 to 14 years in the United States sustain a TBI each
year.16
Children aged 0 to 4 years more commonly experience a TBI and have a poorer prognosis.
The annual death rate from TBI in children younger than 4 years is 5 per 100,000 individuals.
Across all pediatric age groups, TBI occurs more often in boys than girls.17
Pathogenesis
TBI includes closed-head injuries and penetrating head trauma.
In penetrating trauma, the injury typically is caused by direct disruption of brain tissue.
In blunt trauma, the damage is via direct impact and deformation of the skull on underlying
brain tissue or via a contact or noncontact deceleration injury in which the moving brain is
decelerating on the skull’s inner part (coup-contrecoup mechanism).

Pediatric SCI
Overview
SCI is a devastating event that may lead to temporary or permanent impairment of motor,
sensory, or autonomic functions and may have deleterious effects on survival.
Several unique characteristics predispose children to spine injuries that differ from those that
occur in adults.
Children are more predisposed to an upper CSI.33
Children younger than 8 years have more horizontally aligned cervical facets, greater
ligamentous laxity, and a larger head-to-body ratio, all of which predispose them to upper
CSI at the cranial-cervical junction and C1-C2.
The patterns of injury in children older than 10 years are similar to those in adults, including
subaxial cervical and thoracolumbar spine injuries.34
The incidence of pediatric SCI (0 to 17 years) in the United States is estimated to be 17.5 per 1
million individuals.35
72.5% of children with an SCI are boys.
Anatomic Definitions and Considerations
Definitions
The spinal cord extends from the brain stem to the L3 level at birth and to the L1-2 level in
children older than 1 year. It has a unique tract structure (Figure 9).
Conus medullaris is the termination of the spinal cord.
Filum terminale is the residual tissue of the spinal cord that extends from the conus
medullaris to the sacrum.
The thecal sac is the dural-surrounded sac that extends from the spinal cord and contains
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), nerve roots, and the cauda equina.
The cauda equina refers to the nerve roots and filum terminale surrounded by dura that
extends from the spinal cord.

In general, the most common causes of SCI in the pediatric population are MVCs (40.1%),

Approximately 5% of all pediatric head injuries are associated with an SCI.

A primary phase, which occurs at the time of injury (within seconds to minutes postinjury).
A second phase, which usually begins minutes after the injury (and may last for weeks or

Central cord syndrome often is a hyperextension injury mechanism of the cervical spine.
The spinal cord is compressed, and central cord edema occurs. The damage of a more

Overview
Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common progressive spinocerebellar degenerative
disorder.
This disease is characterized by ataxia, which is abnormal, uncoordinated motor activation and
movements.
Non-neurologic manifestations include several orthopaedic, cardiac, and endocrine
associations.
The estimated prevalence is approximately 2 to 4 per 100,000 individuals.46
FRDA is an autosomal recessive disease generated by a mutation in the frataxin gene located
in the long arm of chromosome 9 (9q13-q21).47
Large (66 to 1,500) pathologic triplet repeat expansions of the guanine-adenine-adenine
triplet inhibit the expression of the frataxin gene.
Frataxin proteins are found in mitochondria and are involved in the regulation of iron
metabolism and oxidative stress. Lack of frataxin protein leads to an accumulation of
mitochondrial iron stores, the formation of free radicals, and cell death.
The cerebellar and spinal cord pathways are involved; degeneration mainly affects the neuron
fibers at the corticospinal tracts, spinocerebellar tracts, and posterior columns of the spinal
cord.48

The onset of the disease is related to the number of guanine-adenine-adenine repeats; a
greater number of repeats is associated with an earlier onset of the disease.48
The earlier the onset of disease, the poorer the outcome.

the following:
Ataxia: lack of muscle control or coordination of voluntary movements
Generalized clumsiness
Non-steady wide-based gait
Nystagmus
Dysarthria and dysphagia
Knee and ankle areflexia
Extensor plantar (positive Babinski) response/reflex
Decreased vibration sense

Nerve conduction velocity is slightly decreased in the upper extremities. EMG reveals loss of
motor units and an increase in polyphasic potentials
Management
In addition to an orthopaedic surgeon, the treatment and follow-up of patients with FRDA
should involve a neurologist; cardiologist; endocrinologist; and other health professionals,
such as physical, occupational, and speech therapists.
The use of anesthetic agents in these patients poses a challenge, and an extensive
preoperative evaluation is necessary. In addition, great caution must be exercised in patients
with cardiac conditions if adjusting fluid balance intraoperatively or postoperatively.
Pharmacologic management
Recently, omaveloxolone was approved by the FDA for the management of FRDA in adults
and adolescents aged 16 years or older.
Omaveloxolone targets activation of the Nrf2 pathway, which typically is decreased in cells in
individuals with FRDA. Nrf2 is a cellular defense mechanism that protects against oxidative
stress and neuroinflammation.
Antioxidants, such as Idebenone (a free radical scavenger), are beneficial in patients with
cardiomyopathy.50
Pes cavus, hindfoot-varus correction
Ambulatory patients may be treated via plantar fascia release, tendon lengthening (Achilles
tendon), tendon transfers (tibialis posterior to peroneus brevis), and corrective calcaneal
osteotomies.
Rigid deformities are managed via osteotomy or arthrodesis to achieve a plantigrade foot.
